title: Administration of the CityFHEPS Program for Department of Social Services Homebase Clients
plain_title: Running the CityFHEPS rent subsidy for Homebase clients
agency: New York City Department of Social Services
what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Social Services administers the City Fighting Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (CityFHEPS) program according to the rules, helping residents served by Homebase providers secure permanent housing. The audit covered July 2021 through July 2025.
background: CityFHEPS, launched in 2018, is a rental assistance program for New Yorkers in shelters or at risk of homelessness. Officials say it has helped 123,762 people secure permanent housing through March 2025, with costs rising from $176 million in fiscal year 2019 to $834 million in fiscal year 2024 and projected at $1.2 billion for fiscal year 2025.

findings.plain: Consistent with a prior audit, the department lacks adequate oversight and monitoring of CityFHEPS for people served by Homebase providers, leaving applicants exposed to hazardous apartments and eligibility and payments insufficiently supported.
findings.quote: program applicants were exposed to apartment units with immediately hazardous violations despite preclearance and inspection requirements

findings.plain: In five of 45 sampled cases the department approved units with open hazardous housing violations, including rat and roach infestations. It approved clients for buildings owned by one landlord whose properties had 110 open violations, and it has no landlord disqualification list.
findings.quote: DSS approved CityFHEPS clients to move into three other properties owned by the same landlord with similar issues

findings.plain: Thirty of 75 sampled case records had no evidence that income was verified, so there is no assurance only eligible applicants got the subsidy.
findings.quote: Thirty of 75 CityFHEPS case records sampled showed no evidence that income was verified

findings.plain: The department does not sufficiently verify landlord-broker relationships. In one case it paid $6,800 in broker's fees before finding the landlord and broker shared the same parent company.
findings.quote: DSS paid $6,800 in broker’s fees before later finding that the landlord and broker were both owned by the same parent company

findings.plain: The department could not show it tested whether rents were reasonable in any of 30 sampled Statewide CityFHEPS cases. In 11 of them the approved rent exceeded comparable units, by $525 on average and by as much as $1,647 a month.
findings.quote: DSS officials could not provide evidence that a rent reasonableness test was completed for any of the 30 sampled Statewide CityFHEPS cases

findings.plain: Because of insufficient monitoring of landlord payments and inaccurate tax forms sent to landlords, there is less assurance that accurate rent payments are reported to the Internal Revenue Service.
findings.quote: DSS issuing inaccurate Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 1099s to landlords

People the program has helped secure permanent housing
Average excess of approved rents over comparable units

recommendations: Establish policies and procedures to check for all housing violations during preclearance and expand preclearance checks to all CityFHEPS cases.
Create a landlord disqualification list with written procedures for adding and removing landlords, and monitor for compliance.
Follow eligibility verification policies, including income checks for all household members 18 and older, and keep all eligibility documents.
Develop written procedures, and monitor compliance, to confirm no substantiated relationship exists between landlords, brokers and managing members and that rent payments go to the correct parties.
